title: What is onomatopoeia? Words with their own sound effects
description: Buzz, hiss, pop: some words bring a little noise to the page. Discover onomatopoeia through everyday examples and a kettle with something to say.

sections.title: A big word for small noises
sections.html:
Onomatopoeia is the use or creation of words that imitate the sounds they describe. Think of buzz, hiss or pop: a small sound effect tucked into a word.

Merriam-Webster uses buzz and hiss as examples. The term looks rather grand for something you might hear while making a cup of tea.

sections.title: Give the kettle a line
sections.html:
Compare our two invented sentences: “The kettle made a noise.” “The kettle hissed.”

The second gives your imagination something to listen to. Try the same idea with “The balloon popped” or “The pan sizzled.” Each verb suggests a different noise. You can almost hear the kitchen getting busy, even on a quiet page.

sections.title: A word is not a recording
sections.html:
These words suggest a sound; they do not reproduce every detail of it. Saying pop is not quite the same as bursting a balloon beside someone’s ear.

That is part of their charm in a story. A little hiss can make an otherwise ordinary sentence feel more immediate, without a paragraph explaining the noise.

sections.title: The name has its own story
sections.html:
Oxford traces the term to Greek roots meaning name and making. A long name for a wonderfully direct idea.

If you enjoy what sound does to words, discover why flour and flower sound alike, then meet the spoonerism that turns jelly beans into belly jeans. English can be quite a noisy playground.
